title: How does an API Gateway track request tracing across microservices (trace IDs, Zipkin/OpenTelemetry)?
shortTitle: How an API Gateway tracks request tracing across microservices

s1_definition.profdef: Distributed tracing follows a single request as it travels through many services, so you can see the full path and timing. The gateway is the natural origin of a trace: it generates a trace ID that identifies the whole request, and a span ID for its own unit of work, then propagates these as context, usually W3C `traceparent` headers, to every downstream service. Each service creates child spans under the same trace ID, and all spans are exported to a tracing backend like Zipkin or an OpenTelemetry collector, which stitches them into one timeline. This lets you answer "where did this request spend its time and where did it fail" across service boundaries.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh's loan application at National Bank of India gets a single reference number stamped on it at the front desk. As the application moves from the front desk to verification to credit scoring to approval, every department writes its notes under that same reference number and records when it received and finished the file. Later, a manager pulls that one reference number and sees the complete journey: which department had it, for how long, and where it got stuck. The trace ID is that reference number, and each department's timed note is a span.
s1_definition.oneliner: The gateway mints a trace ID and propagates it in standard headers, every service adds timed child spans under it, and a backend like Zipkin or OpenTelemetry stitches them into one end-to-end timeline.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Distributed tracing follows a single request as it travels through many services, so you can see the full path and timing. The gateway is the natural origin of a trace: it generates a trace ID that identifies the whole request, and a span ID for its own unit of work, then propagates these as context, usually W3C `traceparent` headers, to every downstream service. Each service creates child spans under the same trace ID, and all spans are exported to a tracing backend like Zipkin or an OpenTelemetry collector, which stitches them into one timeline. This lets you answer "where did this request spend its time and where did it fail" across service boundaries.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh's loan application at National Bank of India gets a single reference number stamped on it at the front desk. As the application moves from the front desk to verification to credit scoring to approval, every department writes its notes under that same reference number and records when it received and finished the file. Later, a manager pulls that one reference number and sees the complete journey: which department had it, for how long, and where it got stuck. The trace ID is that reference number, and each department's timed note is a span.

**One line to remember:** The gateway mints a trace ID and propagates it in standard headers, every service adds timed child spans under it, and a backend like Zipkin or OpenTelemetry stitches them into one end-to-end timeline.

sections.s2_technical:
A trace represents one request's whole journey and carries a unique trace ID. Within a trace, each unit of work is a span with its own span ID, a start and end time, and a parent span ID that links it to the span that called it. So a trace is a tree of spans sharing one trace ID. The gateway, being the entry point, is usually where the root span and the trace ID are created.

Context propagation is the mechanism that keeps the trace ID flowing. When the gateway calls a downstream service, it injects the trace context into the request headers, and the downstream service extracts it and continues the same trace. The modern standard is the W3C Trace Context, a header named `traceparent` that encodes the trace ID, the parent span ID, and sampling flags, for example `traceparent: 00-<trace-id>-<span-id>-01`. Because it is a standard, services written in different languages and frameworks interoperate.

In the Spring ecosystem, Micrometer Tracing, which replaced Spring Cloud Sleuth, handles this automatically. It generates and propagates trace and span IDs, puts the trace ID into the logging context so every log line includes it, and bridges to an exporter. For example, with the right dependencies, a log line automatically shows the trace ID, so searching logs for one trace ID returns every log from every service for that one request.

The exporter sends spans to a tracing backend. Zipkin is a popular, simple backend that receives spans and draws the waterfall timeline. OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral standard: your services use the OpenTelemetry SDK to produce spans and send them to an OpenTelemetry Collector, which can then forward to Zipkin, Jaeger, or a commercial backend. Using OpenTelemetry means you are not locked to one tracing vendor.

Sampling controls cost. Tracing every single request in a high-throughput bank would produce an overwhelming volume of span data, so you sample, meaning you fully trace only a fraction of requests. The sampling decision is made once, usually at the gateway, and encoded in the `traceparent` flags so the whole trace is consistently sampled or not. Head-based sampling decides at the start; tail-based sampling, done in the collector, can keep all traces that errored or were slow, which is often what you actually want.

For the gateway specifically, there is a reactive subtlety. In a non-blocking gateway the request hops across threads, so the trace context cannot live in a plain thread-local; it must be carried through the reactive context so the trace ID survives thread switches. Micrometer Tracing and the Reactor context integration handle this, but it is a common source of "lost trace ID" bugs if misconfigured.

A senior nuance is correlation versus tracing. Even without a full tracing backend, simply propagating a correlation ID in a header and logging it everywhere already lets you grep all logs for one request, which is the cheapest useful first step. Full tracing adds the timing and the visual waterfall on top. Another nuance is that you should also propagate baggage, meaning a few business keys like account ID, carefully, because it is useful for debugging but adds overhead and can leak sensitive data if abused.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — When Rajesh complains that his transfer took eight seconds, the support team at National Bank of India needs to know where the time went. The request passed through the gateway, the account service, a fraud-check service, and the payment service. Without a shared trace ID, each service's logs are separate islands and nobody can reconstruct the one request's journey. This is exactly what distributed tracing solves.

Problem 2 — The trace must survive crossing service boundaries. If the gateway creates a trace ID but does not propagate it, each downstream service invents its own and the correlation is lost. So propagation through headers is the essential mechanism, not an optional extra.

The connection to the fix: we will model a trace context that the gateway creates and propagates to each service. Each service creates a child span with timing under the same trace ID and records it. At the end we print the assembled trace as a waterfall, exactly what Zipkin would show.

What the code will do. There is a `TraceContext` holding a trace ID and the current span's ID. There is a `Span` with a service name, a span ID, a parent span ID, and start and end times. There is a `Tracer` that starts and finishes spans and collects them. There are simulated `Gateway`, `AccountService`, `FraudService`, and `PaymentService` that each start a child span, do simulated work, and propagate the same trace context onward. The demo runs one transfer end to end and prints the waterfall of spans sharing one trace ID.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile and run the plain-Java tracing demo
javac TracingDemo.java
java com.bank.gateway.demo.TracingDemo

# Real Spring Boot with Micrometer Tracing + Zipkin running locally
docker run -d -p 9411:9411 openzipkin/zipkin
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/tracing-gateway-service-1.0.0.jar

# Make a request, then view the trace at http://localhost:9411
curl http://localhost:8080/api/v1/transfers -d '{"from":"SAV2001","to":"CUR3001"}'
```
sections.s5_journey:
The input is one transfer request from Rajesh's SAV2001 to Priya's CUR3001 passing through four services.

Step 1. The gateway receives the request and, being the entry point, mints a brand-new trace ID that will identify this whole request. It starts a root span for itself with no parent, and notes the start time. The trace now exists and belongs to this one request.

Step 2. The gateway builds a trace context carrying the trace ID and its own span ID, and calls the account service with that context. In a real system this context would travel as a `traceparent` header. The account service extracts it and starts a child span under the same trace ID, with the gateway's span as its parent. It does its work for about forty milliseconds and finishes its span.

Step 3. The gateway then calls the fraud service with the same context. The fraud service starts another child span under the same trace ID and takes about ninety milliseconds, which turns out to be the slowest step. This is the kind of hotspot tracing is designed to reveal.

Step 4. The gateway calls the payment service with the same context, which starts its own child span under the trace ID and takes about sixty milliseconds. All child spans share one trace ID and point back to the gateway's root span as parent.

Step 5. The gateway finishes its root span. The tracer now holds four spans that all share the same trace ID. Printing them as a waterfall shows the full journey and the time each service took, immediately revealing that the fraud service was the slow part. This is exactly the timeline Zipkin or an OpenTelemetry backend would render for support to diagnose Rajesh's slow transfer.

```
2026-10-24 13:40:01 [INFO] === One transfer traced end to end ===
2026-10-24 13:40:01 [INFO] START span service=api-gateway traceId=00010002 spanId=0003 parent=null
2026-10-24 13:40:01 [INFO] START span service=account-service traceId=00010002 spanId=0004 parent=0003
2026-10-24 13:40:01 [INFO] START span service=fraud-service traceId=00010002 spanId=0005 parent=0003
2026-10-24 13:40:01 [INFO] START span service=payment-service traceId=00010002 spanId=0006 parent=0003
2026-10-24 13:40:01 [INFO] === Assembled trace (Zipkin-style waterfall) ===
2026-10-24 13:40:01 [INFO] [00010002] api-gateway      span=0003 parent=null 200ms
2026-10-24 13:40:01 [INFO]    [00010002] account-service  span=0004 parent=0003 40ms
2026-10-24 13:40:01 [INFO]    [00010002] fraud-service    span=0005 parent=0003 90ms
2026-10-24 13:40:01 [INFO]    [00010002] payment-service  span=0006 parent=0003 60ms
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Client: POST /api/v1/transfers {from:SAV2001, to:CUR3001}
    │
    ▼
  API Gateway  ── mint traceId=00010002, root span=0003 (parent=null)
    │ inject traceparent: 00-00010002-0003-01
    ├───────────────→ Account Service   span=0004 parent=0003  (40ms)
    ├───────────────→ Fraud Service     span=0005 parent=0003  (90ms)  ← slowest
    └───────────────→ Payment Service   span=0006 parent=0003  (60ms)
    │
    ▼  all spans share traceId=00010002
  Exporter → OpenTelemetry Collector → Zipkin/Jaeger
    │
    ▼
  Waterfall timeline:
    api-gateway     |██████████████████| 200ms
      account-svc   |████|               40ms
      fraud-svc     |█████████|          90ms
      payment-svc   |██████|             60ms
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Distributed tracing follows one request as it travels through many services, and the gateway is the natural place where a trace begins. A trace has a single trace ID that identifies the whole request, and within it every unit of work is a span with its own span ID, a parent span ID, and start and end times, so a trace is really a tree of spans sharing one ID. Because the gateway is the entry point, it mints the trace ID and creates the root span, then propagates the trace context to every downstream service, and each service creates child spans under the same trace ID. All of those spans are exported to a backend like Zipkin or an OpenTelemetry collector, which stitches them into one end-to-end timeline.

The mechanism that makes this work is context propagation through headers. The modern standard is the W3C Trace Context, a `traceparent` header that carries the trace ID, the parent span ID, and the sampling decision. Because it is a standard, services in different languages interoperate. In the Spring world, Micrometer Tracing, which replaced Sleuth, does this automatically: it generates and propagates the IDs, puts the trace ID into the logging context so every log line carries it, and bridges to an exporter. That last part is enormously practical, because searching the logs for one trace ID returns every log from every service for that single request.

In my banking work at National Bank of India, this is exactly how we diagnosed a complaint that a transfer took eight seconds. The request passed through the gateway, the account service, a fraud-check service, and the payment service, and before tracing, each service's logs were separate islands. With a shared trace ID propagated from the gateway, we pulled up one trace and immediately saw the waterfall: the fraud-check service was the slow step. Without tracing we would have been guessing; with it, the hotspot was obvious in seconds.

The nuances I always mention are sampling, the reactive subtlety, and the cheap first step. Sampling matters because tracing every request in a high-throughput bank would be an overwhelming volume, so we sample a fraction, and we decide once, usually at the gateway, encoding it in the traceparent so the whole trace is consistent; tail-based sampling in the collector lets us keep all the errored or slow traces, which are the ones we actually care about. The reactive subtlety is that in a non-blocking gateway the request hops across threads, so the trace context must ride the reactive context rather than a thread-local, or the trace ID gets lost. And the cheapest useful first step, even before a full tracing backend, is simply to propagate a correlation ID and log it everywhere, because that alone lets you grep all the logs for one request; full tracing with Zipkin or OpenTelemetry then adds the timing and the visual waterfall on top.
